organic_practices: Implement crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops to reduce pathogen buildup in the soil.
Practice good sanitation by removing and destroying all infected plant debris from the field.
Ensure proper plant spacing to improve air circulation and reduce leaf wetness.
Use disease-free seeds or healthy transplants to prevent initial infection.
Apply organic fungicides such as neem oil extracts or copper-based formulations as preventative measures or at early disease onset.
Utilize biological control agents like Bacillus subtilis which can inhibit fungal growth.

disease_info.cause: Caused by the necrotrophic fungus Alternaria melongenae, which thrives in warm, humid conditions and periods of prolonged leaf wetness. Spores germinate on the leaf surface and directly penetrate the plant tissue, leading to localized cell death.
disease_info.symptoms: Characterized by numerous small, circular to irregular dark brown spots that often develop distinct concentric rings (target-spot appearance) and are surrounded by a yellow halo. Lesions can coalesce to form larger necrotic areas. Severely infected areas may lead to a 'shot-hole' effect as dead tissue falls out. Leaves may yellow and drop prematurely.
disease_info.disease_spread: Primarily spread by wind and rain splash, disseminating spores from infected plant debris, soil, or neighboring diseased plants. Can also be transmitted through infected seeds.

organic_practices: Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops for at least 2-3 years
Remove and destroy all infected plant debris after harvest to reduce inoculum
Ensure proper plant spacing and pruning to improve air circulation and reduce leaf wetness
Use disease-free certified seeds or seedlings
Apply organic fungicides containing Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum as preventive measures
Mulch around plants to prevent soil splash onto lower leaves

disease_info.cause: Caused by the fungus Alternaria solani, which thrives in warm (20-30°C) and humid conditions, especially with prolonged leaf wetness. Spores germinate and infect leaves, stems, and fruits, leading to tissue damage and necrosis.
disease_info.symptoms: Symptoms include the appearance of small, circular to irregular dark brown spots, often with concentric rings (target spot appearance) and a yellow halo, primarily on older leaves. As the disease progresses, spots enlarge, coalesce, and cause large necrotic areas, leading to premature defoliation. Some areas show a 'shot-hole' effect where necrotic tissue has fallen out.
disease_info.disease_spread: The fungus survives on infected plant debris in the soil, on volunteer plants, and perennial weeds. Spores are primarily spread by wind, splashing rain, irrigation water, and agricultural tools or human activity. Infected seeds can also be a source of primary inoculum.

organic_practices: Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops for at least 2-3 years to break the disease cycle.
Remove and destroy all infected plant debris, especially at the end of the growing season.
Ensure proper plant spacing to improve air circulation and reduce leaf wetness periods.
Use drip irrigation or water early in the day at the base of plants to minimize wetting of foliage.
Apply mulches (e.g., straw, shredded leaves) to reduce soil splash onto lower leaves.
Utilize resistant or tolerant brinjal varieties if available.
Apply biofungicides containing Bacillus subtilis, Trichoderma harzianum, or other beneficial microbes.

disease_info.cause: Caused by the fungus Alternaria solani, which overwinters in infected plant debris in the soil or on seeds. It thrives in warm temperatures (24-29°C) and extended periods of leaf wetness from dew, rain, or irrigation, leading to spore germination and infection.
disease_info.symptoms: Characterized by circular to irregular brown spots with distinctive concentric rings (target-like pattern) on older leaves, often surrounded by a yellow halo. As the disease progresses, spots enlarge, coalesce, and can cause significant leaf defoliation. Stem lesions and fruit spots may also occur.
disease_info.disease_spread: Spread primarily by wind, rain splash, irrigation water, and infected plant debris in the soil. It can also be carried on infected seeds or contaminated tools.

treatment: This causes a mushy, water-soaked rot on the head that smells very foul. It spreads fast in warm, wet weather through wounds. To treat, spray Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter) or Streptocycline. Harvest only in dry weather and handle heads carefully to avoid scratches. Clear all plant debris after harvest. Rotating with corn or legumes helps reduce the bacteria in the soil.

organic_practices: Implement a strict 2-3 year crop rotation program, avoiding other Brassica crops.
Remove and destroy all infected plant material immediately to reduce inoculum.
Avoid injuring plants during transplanting, cultivation, and harvest.
Improve soil drainage and avoid overwatering to reduce humidity.
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead irrigation to minimize leaf wetness.
Control insect pests that can create wounds, serving as entry points for bacteria.
Ensure proper plant spacing to improve air circulation.
Sanitize tools and equipment regularly with a bleach solution (10% bleach).
Plant disease-resistant or tolerant cabbage varieties if available.
chemical_practices: Streptomycin (use limited due to resistance development and availability)

disease_info.cause: Bacterial soft rot is primarily caused by several species of bacteria, including Pectobacterium carotovorum. These bacteria produce enzymes that break down pectin, which is the 'glue' holding plant cells together. Infection commonly occurs through wounds (from insects, machinery, or handling) or natural openings like stomata, especially under warm, humid conditions or when the plants are stressed due to waterlogging or nutrient imbalance. The pathogen can also be present in soil or on crop residues.
disease_info.symptoms: Initial symptoms include water-soaked lesions that rapidly expand and become soft, mushy, and discolored (often cream to brown or black). A characteristic foul odor is frequently associated with the decaying tissue. In cabbage heads, the internal leaves become slimy and rot, leading to a complete collapse of the head structure.
disease_info.disease_spread: The bacteria can survive in soil, infected plant debris, and on the surface of tools or machinery. It is primarily spread by splashing water (rain, irrigation), contaminated tools, insects (such as cabbage maggots or other chewing insects that create wounds), and can also be moved through contaminated irrigation water. Wounds on the plant surface provide easy entry points for the pathogen.

treatment: You will see yellow "V-shaped" patches on leaf edges. Spray Streptocycline (1g in 10L) mixed with Copper Oxychloride (20g). Always use "hot water treated" seeds (50°C for 30 mins) to kill hidden bacteria. Avoid working in the field when plants are wet. This is the most serious cabbage disease in India; rotating crops for 2 years is essential.

organic_practices: Use certified disease-free seeds or treat seeds with hot water (50°C for 25-30 minutes) to eliminate seed-borne bacteria.
Practice crop rotation with non-brassica crops for at least 3-4 years to reduce soil inoculum.
Remove and destroy all infected plant debris immediately after harvest to prevent carryover.
Ensure proper field sanitation, including cleaning tools and equipment.
Improve air circulation and avoid overhead irrigation to minimize leaf wetness.
Plant resistant cabbage varieties if available.
chemical_practices: Streptomycin (where permitted and effective against resistant strains)

disease_info.cause: Caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris, which infects the plant through wounds or natural openings like hydathodes at the leaf margins. Once inside, it multiplies and spreads through the vascular system (xylem), causing systemic infection and breakdown of tissues.
disease_info.symptoms: Initial symptoms include V-shaped yellow lesions extending inward from the leaf margins, often turning black. Veins within the lesions become blackened. In severe cases, the entire head may rot, as seen in the image, with internal blackening of vascular tissues.
disease_info.disease_spread: Primarily seed-borne and soil-borne. It can also spread by splashing rain or irrigation water, contaminated farm tools, insect vectors, and movement of infected plant debris.

organic_practices: Maintain good soil health through organic matter addition and cover cropping.
Implement proper irrigation to avoid water stress.
Scout regularly for early signs of pests or nutrient deficiencies.
Practice crop rotation to break potential disease cycles.
Ensure balanced nutrient application based on soil tests.
chemical_practices: Not applicable as no specific disease requiring chemical intervention is identified.

treatment: Large, V-shaped brown spots start from the leaf edge and move inward. It often happens after harvest. Sanitate the field by removing old leaves. If the infection is severe, spray with Carbendazim or Thiophanate-methyl. Since this fungus survives on dead leaves in winter, cleaning your field at the end of the season is the best prevention.

organic_practices: Plant resistant potato varieties if available.
Practice proper crop rotation (3-4 years) with non-solanaceous crops.
Remove and destroy all infected plant debris immediately to reduce inoculum.
Ensure adequate plant spacing for good air circulation to reduce leaf wetness.
Avoid overhead irrigation, especially late in the day, to minimize leaf wetness duration.
Use disease-free certified seed potatoes.
Apply approved organic fungicides (e.g., copper-based products like Bordeaux mixture) preventatively.
Build healthy soil with compost and balanced nutrients to enhance plant vigor.

disease_info.cause: Late blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. It thrives in cool to moderate temperatures (10-25°C or 50-77°F) and high humidity or prolonged leaf wetness. Spores (sporangia) are produced on infected leaves and stems, which are then dispersed by wind and rain to healthy plants, infecting them and rapidly destroying plant tissue.
disease_info.symptoms: Symptoms typically appear as irregular, water-soaked lesions that rapidly expand into large, dark brown to black necrotic spots, often starting at leaf tips or margins. A pale green or yellowish halo may surround the lesions. In humid conditions, a fuzzy, white fungal-like growth (sporangia) can often be seen on the underside of the leaves, especially at the edge of the lesions. Infected stems develop dark, elongated lesions.
disease_info.disease_spread: The disease spreads primarily through wind-borne sporangia, rain splash, movement of infected seed tubers, contaminated soil, and infected plant debris. Spores can also be carried short distances by insects or tools.

Remove and destroy infected plant debris to reduce inoculum.
Use disease-free seeds or healthy transplants.
Ensure proper plant spacing for improved air circulation.
Avoid overhead irrigation, or water early in the day to allow leaves to dry.
Apply organic fungicides like Bordeaux mixture or copper-based sprays.
Utilize biological control agents such as Bacillus subtilis.

disease_info.cause: Caused by the fungus Alternaria alternata, which thrives in warm, humid conditions with prolonged leaf wetness. Spores are released from infected plant debris or other host plants and spread by wind, splashing rain, or irrigation.
disease_info.symptoms: Initial symptoms are small, dark, circular to irregular spots on older leaves, often with concentric rings (target spot appearance) and a yellow halo. As the disease progresses, spots enlarge, coalesce, causing large necrotic areas, blighting, and premature defoliation. Severe infections can lead to stem lesions and fruit rot.
disease_info.disease_spread: The fungus spreads primarily through airborne conidia (spores) carried by wind, splashing rain or irrigation water, and contaminated plant debris. It can also be seed-borne.

organic_practices: Ensure adequate ventilation in storage facilities to provide sufficient oxygen to tubers.
Maintain optimal storage temperatures (typically 3-5°C or 37-41°F) and avoid sudden temperature fluctuations.
Avoid storing tubers in conditions that promote high respiration rates.
Improve soil drainage in fields to prevent waterlogging, especially during tuber development.
Harvest tubers carefully to minimize bruising, which can exacerbate other internal disorders.

disease_info.cause: Blackheart is a physiological disorder caused by a lack of oxygen (anoxia) to the internal potato tuber tissues. This can occur due to inadequate ventilation during storage, high storage temperatures, or waterlogging in the soil before harvest. When oxygen levels are insufficient for respiration, cells die, leading to the characteristic black discoloration.
disease_info.symptoms: Internal tissues, typically in the center of the tuber, turn black and may initially be watery before drying out to form distinct, often irregular, dark cavities. The discoloration is not always uniform and can appear as patches.
disease_info.disease_spread: Not applicable; Blackheart is a physiological disorder and does not spread like a pathogenic disease.
